title: CUET Political Science Test 11
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)

One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Why the UN was set up
questions.question: Why was the United Nations set up in 1945?
options: A) To replace national governments with a world government
B) To prevent conflict and help states cooperate after the war
C) To divide the colonies among the victorious powers
D) To create a single currency for all its members
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To prevent conflict and help states cooperate after the war
Why: After the failure of the League of Nations and the devastation of the Second World War, the UN was set up to prevent conflict and promote cooperation.
Why not the others:
(A) The UN is an organisation of sovereign states.
(C) The UN supported decolonisation.
(D) The UN has no currency.
Key point: The UN grew out of the lessons of two world wars.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Areas of India–Russia cooperation besides defence
questions.question: Besides defence, Russia has helped India in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nuclear energy and space
Why: Russia has helped India in its nuclear energy and space programmes.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) have nothing to do with Russia.
Key point: India–Russia ties cover many strategic areas.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Why East Pakistan resented West Pakistan
questions.question: Why did the people of East Pakistan come to resent West Pakistan's rule?
options: A) Urdu was imposed on them and they were treated unfairly.
B) West Pakistan refused to let them trade with India.
C) West Pakistan had given their province to Burma.
D) They were not allowed to follow any religion.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Urdu was imposed on them and they were treated unfairly.
Why: People in East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination and the imposition of Urdu, and were denied their fair share of power.
Why not the others:
(B) Trade with India was not the cause.
(C) No territory was given to Burma.
(D) Religious freedom was not the issue.
Key point: Language and unequal treatment led to Bangladesh.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Threats faced by Third World states
questions.question: How did the security problems of newly independent Third World countries differ from those of Western countries?
options: A) They faced threats from within as well as from neighbours.
B) They faced no threats of any kind after gaining independence.
C) They faced threats only from the two superpowers of the time.
D) They faced threats only from distant countries overseas.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) They faced threats from within as well as from neighbours.
Why: Third World states faced threats from neighbours and also from within, such as separatist movements.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are wrong; their threats were both internal and external.
Key point: For new states, internal security was as pressing as external.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Secretaries-General in the order they took office
questions.question:
Arrange the following Secretaries-General in the order in which they took office:
(A) Ban Ki-moon
(B) U Thant
(C) Boutros Boutros-Ghali
(D) Trygve Lie
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (B), (C), (A)
Why: (D) Trygve Lie was the first Secretary-General (1946). (B) U Thant took office in 1961. (C) Boutros-Ghali in 1992. (A) Ban Ki-moon in 2007.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Boutros-Ghali before U Thant. Option (B) puts U Thant before Trygve Lie. Option (C) puts Ban Ki-moon before Boutros-Ghali.
Key point: 1946 → 1961 → 1992 → 2007.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Ways of managing military rivalry
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Disarmament
(B) Arms control
(C) Confidence building
(D) Balance of power

List-II
(I) Regulating the acquisition or development of weapons
(II) Sharing information about military intentions with rivals
(III) Making sure that no rival becomes too powerful
(IV) Giving up certain kinds of weapons altogether
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Disarmament means giving up certain weapons (IV). Arms control regulates weapons (I). Confidence building means sharing military information (II). Balance of power keeps any rival from becoming too strong (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps disarmament and arms control. Option (B) swaps arms control and confidence building. Option (D) swaps confidence building and balance of power.
Key point: Cooperation can reduce the risk of war.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Why the Syndicate backed Indira Gandhi in 1966
questions.question: Why did the Syndicate support Indira Gandhi for Prime Minister in 1966?
options: A) She had led the Congress to victory in the 1962 election.
B) She was the most experienced minister in the cabinet.
C) They expected her to be inexperienced and depend on them.
D) She had promised to make Kamaraj her deputy minister.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They expected her to be inexperienced and depend on them.
Why: The Syndicate leaders thought that, being inexperienced, she would depend on them for guidance.
Why not the others:
(A) Nehru led the Congress in 1962.
(B) She had little ministerial experience.
(D) NCERT mentions no such promise.
Key point: The Syndicate misjudged her, and she soon asserted herself.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Neo-liberalism, technology and the WSF — spot the error
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Neo-liberal thinking favours the market over the state in economic matters.
(B) India had no contact with global trade or ideas before 1991.
(C) Some argue that new technology has actually increased the capacity of states.
(D) The World Social Forum brings together activists for human rights, the environment, labour, youth and women.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: India had long-standing trade and cultural links with the world well before 1991.
Why not the others: (A) neo-liberals prefer the market. (C) states can use technology to collect information and govern. (D) the WSF is a broad coalition. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Globalisation in India has a long history.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Superpower status after 1991
questions.question: What did the break-up of the Soviet Union mean for the balance of power in the world?
options: A) The US was left as the only superpower.
B) China became the only superpower at once.
C) The EU replaced the US as the main power.
D) The world was split into three equal blocs.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The US was left as the only superpower.
Why: With the Soviet Union gone, the US became the sole superpower.
Why not the others:
(B) China was not a superpower in 1991.
(C) The EU did not replace the US.
(D) No three-bloc system emerged.
Key point: Bipolarity gave way to US dominance.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: How China's path differed from Russia's
questions.question: How did China's move towards a market economy differ from Russia's?
options: A) China privatised everything in a single year.
B) China opened up step by step without shock therapy.
C) China followed the IMF's shock therapy more strictly.
D) China closed its economy to all foreign investment.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) China opened up step by step without shock therapy.
Why: China did not go for shock therapy; it opened its economy gradually, beginning with agriculture and special economic zones.
Why not the others:
(A) and (C) describe shock therapy, which China avoided.
(D) China welcomed foreign investment.
Key point: Gradual reform helped China grow fast.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: The North-East's link to the rest of India
questions.question: The North-East is connected to the rest of India by a narrow corridor about how wide?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 22 km
Why: NCERT notes that the region is linked to the rest of India by a narrow corridor of about 22 km.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not match NCERT's figure.
Key point: Isolation added to the region's sense of neglect.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Popular name of Operation Flood
questions.question: Operation Flood, which made India a leading producer of milk, is often called the ________ Revolution.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) White
Why: The rapid growth in milk production through cooperatives is known as the White Revolution.
Why not the others:
(B) The Green Revolution was about foodgrains.
(C) and (D) do not refer to milk.
Key point: Cooperatives like Amul led the dairy revolution.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: The Emergency and its aftermath — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The cabinet was informed of the Emergency only after it had been proclaimed.
(B) The Lok Sabha elections due in 1976 were postponed during the Emergency.
(C) During the Emergency, citizens could still go to court to enforce their fundamental rights.
(D) In 1977 the Congress lost power at the Centre for the first time.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the right to move the courts to enforce fundamental rights was suspended.
Why not the others: (A) the President proclaimed the Emergency on the PM's advice and the cabinet was told afterwards. (B) the term of the Lok Sabha was extended and elections postponed. (D) 1977 was the first defeat of the Congress at the Centre. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The Emergency suspended key democratic safeguards.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Shape of national politics by the 2000s
questions.question: By the 2000s, national politics had largely become a contest between:
options: A) the Congress and the Communist parties alone
B) a large number of small parties with no alliances
C) regional parties that refused to join any coalition
D) two coalitions led by the Congress and the BJP
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) two coalitions led by the Congress and the BJP
Why: Elections came to be fought mainly between the UPA, led by the Congress, and the NDA, led by the BJP.
Why not the others:
(A) The Communists were one part of the picture.
(B) Parties formed alliances.
(C) Regional parties joined both coalitions.
Key point: Coalition politics became the norm.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: How the restored Congress differed from Nehru's
questions.question: Why does NCERT say the Congress system was 'restored' after 1971 only in a different form?
options: A) The party now depended on one leader's popular appeal.
B) The party had merged with the Swatantra and Jana Sangh.
C) The party had stopped contesting elections in the States.
D) The party had given up its socialist slogans completely.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The party now depended on one leader's popular appeal.
Why: The new Congress relied heavily on Indira Gandhi's popularity and had a weaker organisation, unlike the broad, faction-tolerant party of Nehru's time.
Why not the others:
(B) These parties were its opponents.
(C) It still contested in the States.
(D) It had campaigned on socialist slogans like garibi hatao.
Key point: Dominance returned, but the party's character had changed.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Nehru's view on nuclear weapons
questions.question: What was Nehru's stand on nuclear weapons?
options: A) He wanted India to test a bomb at the earliest.
B) He supported the nuclear monopoly of the West.
C) He called for complete nuclear disarmament.
D) He asked the Soviet Union for a nuclear shield.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He called for complete nuclear disarmament.
Why: Nehru opposed nuclear weapons and pressed for comprehensive nuclear disarmament, while building nuclear energy for peaceful use.
Why not the others:
(A) India's first test came in 1974, after Nehru.
(B) He opposed the big powers' monopoly.
(D) He sought no nuclear shield.
Key point: India's nuclear programme began with a peaceful aim.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Soviet life and the transition — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Soviet citizens had good education and health care but faced shortages of consumer goods.
(B) Gorbachev was criticised by some for moving too fast and by others for moving too slowly.
(C) Shock therapy broke up the collective farm system and hurt food security.
(D) Russia joined NATO soon after the Soviet Union broke up.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the system gave welfare but lagged in consumer goods. (B) hardliners thought he went too far, reformers that he was too slow. (C) the collective farms collapsed and food security suffered.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Russia never joined NATO. Options (B) and (C) include (D); option (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: Reform satisfied neither side and the transition was painful.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Accession, merger and new States, 1947–2014, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Telangana State is formed
(B) The Maharaja of Kashmir signs the Instrument of Accession
(C) Manipur is merged into India
(D) Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand are created
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (C), (D), (A)
Why: (B) Hari Singh signed in October 1947. (C) Manipur was merged in 1949. (D) The three new States were created in 2000. (A) Telangana was formed in 2014.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts Manipur's merger before Kashmir's accession. Option (C) puts 2000 before 1949. Option (D) puts Telangana before the three States of 2000.
Key point: 1947 → 1949 → 2000 → 2014.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Lok Sabha elections and their outcomes
questions.question:
Match List-I (Election) with List-II (Outcome).

List-I
(A) 1991
(B) 1996
(C) 1999
(D) 2009

List-II
(I) The NDA came to power and completed a full five-year term
(II) The UPA returned to power for a second term
(III) The BJP became the largest party, but its government lasted 13 days
(IV) The Congress formed a minority government
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: In 1991 the Congress formed a minority government (IV). In 1996 the BJP's government lasted 13 days (III). In 1999 the NDA won and completed its term (I). In 2009 the UPA returned (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps 1991 and 1996. Option (B) swaps 1996 and 1999. Option (D) swaps 1999 and 2009.
Key point: Coalitions led by the Congress and the BJP alternated in power.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Leaders and countries in the new centres of power
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Mao Zedong
(B) Deng Xiaoping
(C) Japan
(D) Britain

List-II
(I) Stayed out of the euro and later left the EU
(II) Led the communist revolution in China in 1949
(III) The only Asian member of the G-7
(IV) Announced the 'open door' policy in 1978
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Mao led the 1949 revolution (II). Deng announced the open door policy (IV). Japan is the only Asian member of the G-7 (III). Britain stayed out of the euro and later left the EU (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Mao and Deng. Option (C) swaps Deng and Japan. Option (D) swaps Japan and Britain.
Key point: China's path changed from Mao's planning to Deng's reforms.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Landlocked countries of South Asia
questions.question: Which two South Asian countries are landlocked?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Nepal and Bhutan
Why: Nepal and Bhutan have no coastline.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) all have coastlines.
Key point: Landlocked Nepal and Bhutan depend on India for access to the sea.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Tamil Nadu and Goa, 1949–1967, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The DMK forms a government in Madras
(B) Goa is freed from Portuguese rule
(C) An agitation against Hindi as the official language sweeps Madras
(D) The DMK is founded
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (C), (A)
Why: (D) The DMK was founded in 1949. (B) Goa was liberated in 1961. (C) The anti-Hindi agitation took place in 1965. (A) The DMK came to power in 1967.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts Goa's liberation before the DMK's founding. Option (C) puts the anti-Hindi agitation before Goa. Option (D) puts the DMK government before the agitation.
Key point: 1949 → 1961 → 1965 → 1967.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Demand of the Punjabi Suba movement
questions.question: The 'Punjabi Suba' movement demanded:
options: A) the return of Lahore from Pakistan
B) the merger of Punjab and Haryana
C) a separate country called Khalistan
D) a State for Punjabi speakers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a State for Punjabi speakers
Why: The movement sought a Punjabi-speaking State, which led to the creation of Punjab and Haryana in 1966.
Why not the others:
(A) The movement did not demand Lahore.
(B) It sought to separate the Punjabi-speaking areas, not merge them.
(C) The Khalistan demand arose much later.
Key point: Linguistic reorganisation continued well after 1956.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: The Janata government's foreign policy
questions.question: What did the Janata government of 1977 promise in foreign policy?
options: A) To join a military alliance with the United States
C) To end all ties with the Soviet Union
D) To leave the United Nations
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To follow 'genuine' non-alignment
Why: The Janata government said it would follow genuine non-alignment, suggesting the previous government had tilted towards the Soviet Union.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) were not part of its policy.
Key point: Broad agreement on foreign policy survived changes of government.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Not a principal organ of the UN
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the principal organs of the United Nations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) UNICEF
Why: UNICEF is a specialised agency working for children, not a principal organ.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are principal organs, along with the Security Council, ECOSOC and the Trusteeship Council.
Key point: The UN has six principal organs and many agencies.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: India's development model — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The First Five Year Plan sought to pull the economy out of the cycle of poverty.
(B) The public sector was given a leading role in heavy industries such as steel and power.
(C) Agriculture, trade and much of industry remained in private hands.
(D) The Green Revolution was launched in the early 1950s along with the First Plan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the First Plan aimed to break the cycle of poverty. (B) the state led in heavy industry. (C) agriculture, trade and much industry stayed private, making the economy mixed.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the Green Revolution began in the mid-1960s, after the food crisis. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: India chose a mixed economy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: When the BJP turned to Hindu nationalism
questions.question: From about when did the BJP begin to stress Hindu nationalism and the Ayodhya issue?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) After 1986
Why: NCERT says that from 1986 the BJP began to emphasise Hindu nationalism, taking up the Ayodhya issue.
Why not the others:
(B) The BJP did not exist in 1951; the Jana Sangh was founded then.
(C) The BJP was founded only in 1980.
(D) The shift came long before 2004.
Key point: Hindutva helped the BJP grow rapidly after the mid-1980s.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Party NOT part of the Janata Party
questions.question: Which of the following did NOT join the Janata Party formed before the 1977 election?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Communist Party of India
Why: The CPI had supported the Emergency and did not join the Janata Party.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C), along with the Socialist Party, came together to form the Janata Party.
Key point: Opposition to the Emergency united very different parties.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Not a feature of economic globalisation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of economic globalisation?
options: A) Greater flow of trade between countries
B) Easier movement of capital across borders
C) Reduced barriers to foreign investment
D) Closing borders to all foreign goods
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Closing borders to all foreign goods
Why: Economic globalisation removes barriers to trade and investment; closing borders is the opposite.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are features of economic globalisation.
Key point: Economic globalisation means more open economies.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Use of force in cooperative security
questions.question: What does NCERT say about the use of force in cooperative security?
options: A) Force is never allowed under any circumstances.
B) Force is the first and preferred means of action.
C) Force can be used only by a single superpower.
D) Force may be used, but only as a last resort.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Force may be used, but only as a last resort.
Why: Cooperative security prefers non-violent means, but force may be used as a last resort, for example against terrorists.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) misstate the approach.
Key point: Cooperation comes first; force is a last resort.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Criticism of Agenda 21
questions.question: What criticism was made of Agenda 21, adopted at the Earth Summit?
options: A) It favoured economic growth over ecological conservation.
B) It forced developing countries to stop all industry.
C) It banned the use of oil in every member country.
D) It handed control of forests to the United Nations.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It favoured economic growth over ecological conservation.
Why: Critics said Agenda 21 was biased in favour of economic growth rather than ensuring ecological conservation.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not what Agenda 21 did.
Key point: Sustainable development means balancing growth and the environment.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Terms in the politics of religion and caste
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Ram Janmabhoomi
(B) Dalit
(C) Reservation
(D) Rath yatra

List-II
(I) Advani's journey to mobilise support for the Ayodhya temple
(II) A quota of seats in jobs and education for disadvantaged groups
(III) The belief that the site at Ayodhya was Rama's birthplace
(IV) A term meaning 'oppressed', used by the lowest castes for themselves
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Ram Janmabhoomi is the belief about Rama's birthplace (III). Dalit means 'oppressed' (IV). Reservation is a quota (II). The rath yatra was Advani's mobilisation (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Ram Janmabhoomi and Dalit. Option (C) swaps Dalit and reservation. Option (D) swaps reservation and the rath yatra.
Key point: Caste and religion became central to politics in the 1990s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Turning points in South Asia, 1948–1990, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Sri Lanka becomes independent
(B) An attempted coup in the Maldives is foiled with India's help
(C) Nepal adopts a democratic constitution
(D) Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman is assassinated
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (D), (B), (C)
Why: (A) Sri Lanka became independent in 1948. (D) Mujib was killed in 1975. (B) The Maldives coup was foiled in 1988. (C) Nepal's democratic constitution came in 1990.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Maldives coup before Mujib's death. Option (B) puts Mujib's death before Sri Lanka's independence. Option (D) puts Nepal before the Maldives.
Key point: 1948 → 1975 → 1988 → 1990.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Leaders and defectors of the 1960s
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Atulya Ghosh
(B) C.N. Annadurai
(C) Gaya Lal
(D) Charan Singh

List-II
(I) Haryana MLA whose defections gave rise to the phrase 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram'
(II) Syndicate leader from West Bengal
(III) Led the DMK to power in Madras in 1967
(IV) Left the Congress and became Chief Minister of UP in 1967
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why: Atulya Ghosh was a Syndicate leader from Bengal (II). Annadurai led the DMK to power in 1967 (III). Gaya Lal's defections gave the phrase 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram' (I). Charan Singh left the Congress and became UP Chief Minister (IV).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Ghosh and Annadurai. Option (B) swaps Annadurai and Gaya Lal. Option (C) swaps Gaya Lal and Charan Singh.
Key point: 1967 saw defections and the rise of non-Congress governments.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: What indigenous peoples demand
questions.question: What do indigenous peoples' movements mainly demand?
options: A) Separate armies for each community
B) The right to rule over other groups
C) Rights to their land and resources
D) Free migration to industrial countries
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rights to their land and resources
Why: Indigenous peoples demand the right to their land and resources and to be treated as equals.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not their demands.
Key point: Development projects often displace indigenous peoples.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Status of the state under globalisation
questions.question: Despite globalisation, NCERT says that the state:
options: A) has disappeared in most developed countries
B) has handed all its powers to multinational companies
C) is now governed directly by the World Trade Organisation
D) remains the main basis of political community
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) remains the main basis of political community
Why: NCERT says the state continues to be the unchallenged basis of political community, even if its role has changed.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) overstate the decline of the state.
Key point: Globalisation changes the state but does not end it.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: The UN and its reform — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) UN reform covers both its structures and processes and the issues it deals with.
(B) The UN is needed because problems like terrorism and climate change cannot be solved by one country.
(C) The non-permanent members of the Security Council are elected by the General Assembly.
(D) The Secretary-General can veto the decisions of the Security Council.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) NCERT describes two kinds of reform. (B) global problems need a global body. (C) the General Assembly elects the non-permanent members.
Why not the others: (D) is false: only the five permanent members have a veto; the Secretary-General has none. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: The UN remains the main forum for global problems.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Commons and their protection
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Sacred groves
(B) Outer space
(C) Earth's atmosphere
(D) Antarctica

List-II
(I) Patches of forest protected by communities in India
(II) Set aside for peaceful scientific research by a treaty of 1959
(III) Its ozone layer is protected by the Montreal Protocol
(IV) Its use is shaped by the technology gap between North and South
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: Sacred groves are community-protected forests (I). The use of outer space is shaped by the technology gap (IV). The atmosphere's ozone layer is protected by the Montreal Protocol (III). Antarctica is reserved for peaceful research under the 1959 treaty (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps sacred groves and outer space. Option (C) swaps outer space and the atmosphere. Option (D) swaps the atmosphere and Antarctica.
Key point: Shared resources need shared rules.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Conflicts ASEAN helped to end
questions.question: Which conflicts has ASEAN helped to bring to an end?
options: A) The Korean War and the Vietnam War
B) The Gulf War and the Iraq War
C) The Kashmir dispute and the Tamil conflict
D) The Cambodian conflict and the East Timor crisis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Cambodian conflict and the East Timor crisis
Why: NCERT says ASEAN mediated the end of the Cambodian conflict and the East Timor crisis.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) were not ended by ASEAN.
Key point: ASEAN's informal approach has helped keep peace in Southeast Asia.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: South Asian politics — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) India and Pakistan fought wars in 1947–48, 1965 and 1971.
(B) Bhutan is still a monarchy.
(C) Bangladesh was one of the founding members of SAARC.
(D) Citizens of India and Nepal need passports and visas to visit each other's country.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: India and Nepal have an open border, and their citizens travel without visas.
Why not the others: (A) these three wars were fought. (B) Bhutan remains a monarchy, though moving towards democracy. (C) Bangladesh was a founding member of SAARC in 1985. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: India–Nepal ties are unusually close.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: JP's appeal that alarmed the government
questions.question: Which appeal by Jayaprakash Narayan in June 1975 was cited by the government as a reason for the Emergency?
options: A) A call for Indira Gandhi to join his movement at once
B) A call to the army and police not to obey illegal orders
C) A call to all the States to secede from the Indian Union
D) A call for foreign powers to intervene in Indian affairs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A call to the army and police not to obey illegal orders
Why: JP called on the army, the police and government employees not to obey 'illegal and immoral' orders, which the government said threatened stability.
Why not the others:
(A) JP demanded her resignation.
(C) JP called for no secession.
(D) No foreign intervention was sought.
Key point: The government claimed a threat to internal security.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: The EU's weight in world trade
questions.question: According to NCERT, how does the EU's share of world trade compare with that of the US?
options: A) It is about one-third of the US share.
B) It is exactly equal to the US share.
C) It is about three times the US share.
D) It is too small to be compared at all.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It is about three times the US share.
Why: NCERT says the EU's share of world trade is three times larger than that of the US.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) contradict this.
Key point: The EU is a major economic power.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Toll of the Partition violence
questions.question: According to estimates given in NCERT, about how many people were killed in the violence of Partition?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Between 5 and 10 lakh
Why: NCERT says estimates of the number killed range from five to ten lakh.
Why not the others:
(A) The toll was far higher.
(B) The number killed was much lower than one crore.
(D) About 80 lakh is the number of people who migrated.
Key point: Partition was one of the largest and bloodiest migrations in history.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: What was unusual about the National Front's support
questions.question: What was unusual about the support for the National Front government formed in 1989?
options: A) It was backed from outside by both the BJP and the Left.
B) It was the first government to have a majority of its own.
C) It was supported by the Congress from inside the cabinet.
D) It was formed with the help of the President's nominees.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It was backed from outside by both the BJP and the Left.
Why: The National Front was supported from outside by two opposed forces, the BJP and the Left parties.
Why not the others:
(B) It had no majority of its own.
(C) The Congress was the main opposition.
(D) No such nominees exist.
Key point: Opposition to the Congress brought unlikely allies together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Russia's economy in 1999 compared with 1989
questions.question: After shock therapy, the value of Russia's GDP in 1999 was ________ than it had been in 1989.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) lower
Why: NCERT notes that Russia's GDP in 1999 was below its 1989 level.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) contradict NCERT's account of economic decline.
Key point: The transition brought a deep economic crisis.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: When the first general election was held
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

India's first general election was a task without precedent. The country had to draw the boundaries of constituencies, prepare electoral rolls for every adult and train lakhs of officials, and the election had to be postponed twice before it could be held. Voting finally took place over several months, between October 1951 and February 1952. Only about 15 per cent of the voters were literate, so special methods had to be found to let people who could not read cast their votes. Many observers, at home and abroad, doubted that a poor and largely illiterate country could choose its government through the ballot. One editor called the exercise the biggest gamble in history, and some predicted that the country would soon fall back on rule by a strong leader or the army. Yet the election was held peacefully, more than half of the eligible voters took part, and the results were accepted as fair even by those who lost. The experience showed that democracy could take root in conditions that many had thought unsuitable, and it became a landmark in the history of democracy all over the world.

Question: According to the passage, over which period did voting in the first general election take place?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) October 1951 to February 1952
Why: The passage says voting took place between October 1951 and February 1952.
Why not the others:
(A) The Constitution came into force in January 1950; no election was held then.
(B) This is the period just after independence.
(D) The election was over by February 1952.
Key point: The first election was spread over several months.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Why the first election was postponed
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Why, according to the passage, did the first election have to be postponed twice?
options: A) Huge preparations like rolls and constituencies were needed.
B) The Congress wanted more time to choose its candidates.
C) The Constitution did not yet allow elections to be held.
D) Voters had refused to take part until literacy improved.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Huge preparations like rolls and constituencies were needed.
Why: The passage lists drawing constituencies, preparing rolls for every adult and training officials as the huge tasks involved.
Why not the others:
(B) The passage does not blame any party.
(C) The passage does not say this.
(D) The passage says more than half the voters took part.
Key point: The scale of preparation was enormous.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: What the passage says about the voters
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: What does the passage say about the voters in the first election?
options: A) Most of them had voted in provincial elections before.
B) Only about 15 per cent of them could read and write.
C) Only men who owned property were allowed to vote.
D) Fewer than one in five eligible voters took part.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only about 15 per cent of them could read and write.
Why: The passage says only about 15 per cent of the voters were literate.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says nothing of earlier experience.
(C) Every adult was entitled to vote.
(D) More than half the voters took part.
Key point: Mass illiteracy did not stop democracy from working.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Account of the 1952 polls — the inconsistent option
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Which of these is at odds with the account given in the passage?
options: A) Some observers expected India to turn to rule by a strong leader.
B) The election was held peacefully across the country.
C) Special methods were used for voters who could not read.
D) The losing parties refused to accept the results as fair.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The losing parties refused to accept the results as fair.
Why: The passage says the results were accepted as fair even by those who lost, so (D) contradicts it.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are each stated in the passage.
Key point: Acceptance of results by the losers is the mark of a working democracy.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: What the first election proved
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The experience showed that democracy could take root in conditions that many had thought unsuitable, and it became a landmark in the history of democracy all over the world.

Question: What can best be concluded from the passage about the first general election?
options: A) It showed that elections should be held only in literate societies.
B) It proved that the army had to supervise elections in poor countries.
C) It proved wrong those who doubted that democracy could work in India.
D) It showed that India should return to indirect election of the Lok Sabha.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It proved wrong those who doubted that democracy could work in India.
Why: The passage contrasts the doubters' predictions with a peaceful, fair election that showed democracy could take root in India.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says the opposite.
(B) The army had no role in the election.
(D) The Lok Sabha was directly elected, and the passage praises this.
Key point: 1951–52 became a landmark for democracy worldwide.
